misconceptions: NULL = NULL is true
WHERE can filter on the result of an aggregate
A LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched rows even when the right table is filtered in WHERE
COUNT(column) counts NULLs

templates.question: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN. Why can a condition placed in WHERE instead of ON change the result of a LEFT JOIN?
keyPoints: An inner join returns only rows that match on both sides
A left join keeps every row of the left table, with NULLs for the right columns where nothing matches
A full outer join keeps unmatched rows of both tables
A WHERE condition on the right table runs after the join and removes the NULL-extended rows, turning the left join into an inner join
Filters on the right table that should keep unmatched rows belong in the ON clause

templates.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? Write a query that finds the customers with more than five orders in the last month.
keyPoints: Logical order: FROM and JOIN, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation
WHERE order_date >= now() - interval '1 month' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
Every selected column that is not aggregated must be in GROUP BY

templates.question: How do window functions differ from GROUP BY? How would you get each customer's most recent order?
keyPoints: A window function computes over rows related to the current row without collapsing them (OVER, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY)
GROUP BY collapses each group into one row
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC), then keep row number 1 in an outer query or CTE
Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, so they cannot be filtered in the same WHERE
PostgreSQL also offers DISTINCT ON (customer_id) with a matching ORDER BY

templates.question: A report query with WHERE status <> 'CANCELLED' is missing the orders whose status is NULL, and another query using NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows at all. Why?
keyPoints: A comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN, not true, so rows with a NULL status are filtered out
Use IS NULL, IS DISTINCT FROM or COALESCE when NULLs must be kept
If the NOT IN subquery returns a NULL, every comparison is UNKNOWN and no row qualifies
NOT EXISTS does not have this problem
COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows

templates.question: You need the three products with the highest revenue in each category. How would you write that query, and why?
keyPoints: Aggregate the revenue per product first (SUM of quantity times price, grouped by product and category)
Rank within each category with a window function partitioned by category and ordered by revenue descending
Keep the rows with rank 3 or less in an outer query or CTE
Choose ROW_NUMBER, RANK or DENSE_RANK depending on how ties should count
CTEs make the steps readable

misconceptions: Foreign keys are only documentation
Normalised schemas are always slow
Floating-point columns are fine for money
A surrogate key makes unique constraints on natural keys unnecessary

templates.question: What is normalization, and which problems do first, second and third normal form prevent?
keyPoints: Normalization stores each fact once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies
First normal form: atomic values and no repeating groups
Second normal form: no attribute depends on only part of a composite key
Third normal form: no attribute depends on another non-key attribute (no transitive dependencies)
Example: a customer's address repeated on every order row goes out of sync when it changes

templates.question: What are primary keys, foreign keys and unique constraints for, and why enforce them in the database rather than only in application code?
keyPoints: A primary key identifies a row; it is unique and not null
A foreign key enforces referential integrity: no orphaned rows, with a defined ON DELETE behaviour
A unique constraint protects natural keys such as an email address even when the table has a surrogate id
Database constraints hold for every client and under concurrency, while an application check-then-insert has a race condition

templates.question: An order-history page joins six tables and is slow. A teammate proposes copying the customer name and product title into the orders table. When is that reasonable, and what do you have to handle?
keyPoints: Denormalization trades write complexity and storage for faster reads
Check the query plans and indexes before restructuring
Some copies are facts of their own: the product title at the time of purchase belongs to the order
Copies that must stay current need to be kept in sync on every change
Alternatives: a materialised view, a read model, or caching

templates.question: Invoice totals are sometimes off by a cent. The amounts are stored in a DOUBLE PRECISION column and summed in SQL. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: Binary floating-point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums accumulate rounding errors
Use NUMERIC (DECIMAL) with a fixed scale, or integer minor units such as cents
Use BigDecimal or an equivalent in the application code
Define the rounding rules explicitly, and convert the existing data carefully

subtopics: When an index is not used
misconceptions: More indexes always make the database faster
An index on (a, b) also serves queries that filter only on b
The database uses an index whenever one exists on the filtered column

templates.question: How does a B-tree index speed up a query, and what does an index cost?
keyPoints: A balanced tree of sorted keys with pointers to the rows finds a key in O(log n) instead of scanning the table
It supports equality, ranges and ORDER BY on the indexed columns
Every insert, update and delete must also maintain each index, which costs write time and storage
Unused indexes are pure cost, and columns with few distinct values gain little

templates.question: Why does the column order of a composite index on (customer_id, created_at) matter? Which queries can use it?
keyPoints: The index is sorted by customer_id first and by created_at within each customer
It serves WHERE customer_id = ? and WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ?, and the ORDER BY created_at of one customer
It does not serve a filter on created_at alone efficiently (leftmost prefix rule)
Put columns compared for equality before columns compared by range
INCLUDE columns can make it a covering index for an index-only scan

templates.subtopic: When an index is not used
templates.question: A query filtering on email is slow although email has an index, and EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. What could cause it?
keyPoints: The query wraps the column in a function or cast, such as lower(email), so an expression index on lower(email) is needed
A type mismatch forces a cast on the column
A pattern with a leading wildcard (LIKE '%x') cannot use a B-tree
For a small table, or a filter that matches many rows, a sequential scan is cheaper
Stale statistics mislead the planner: run ANALYZE and check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE

templates.question: Users search products by name with ILIKE '%term%' and filter by attributes stored in a jsonb column. Which index types would you consider in PostgreSQL?
keyPoints: A B-tree cannot serve a pattern with a leading wildcard
A trigram index (pg_trgm) with GIN or GiST supports ILIKE '%term%'
A GIN index on the jsonb column supports containment queries (@>)
Full-text search with tsvector and a GIN index suits searching for words
Partial indexes cover frequently filtered subsets; check every choice with EXPLAIN ANALYZE

misconceptions: EXPLAIN shows the real execution time
An index scan is always better than a sequential scan
The planner knows the actual row counts in advance

templates.question: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL, and what do you look for in the output for a slow query?
keyPoints: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with estimated costs and row counts without running the query
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and adds the actual time, rows and loops per node; run writes inside a transaction you roll back
Large differences between estimated and actual rows point to bad estimates
Look for the most expensive nodes: sequential scans of large tables, nested loops over many rows, sorts spilling to disk
The BUFFERS option shows how much data was read

templates.question: PostgreSQL can join with a nested loop, a hash join or a merge join. When is each a good choice?
keyPoints: Nested loop: for each outer row look up the inner side, ideally with an index; good when the outer side is small
Hash join: build a hash table on the smaller input and probe it; good for large equality joins, limited by work_mem
Merge join: walk two inputs sorted on the join key; good for large inputs that are already sorted or indexed
The planner chooses by its row estimates and costs

templates.question: After a bulk import, a query that took milliseconds now takes minutes. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows 1 row estimated and 500,000 actual for one node. What happened, and what do you do?
keyPoints: The planner's statistics are stale after the large data change, so its row estimates are far off
A bad estimate leads to a bad plan, such as a nested loop over half a million rows
Run ANALYZE on the table; autovacuum may not have caught up yet
For correlated columns create extended statistics; for skewed data raise the statistics target

templates.question: A dashboard query counts orders per status for the last 7 days in a table of 50 million rows and takes 20 seconds. How would you make it fast?
keyPoints: Read the plan with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) first
An index on created_at, or on (created_at, status), lets it read only the recent rows
An index-only scan needs a covering index and a recently vacuumed table
Partition very large tables by time
If the query runs often, pre-aggregate in a summary table or materialised view

misconceptions: READ COMMITTED prevents lost updates
In PostgreSQL readers block writers
SERIALIZABLE in PostgreSQL works by locking whole tables

templates.question: What do the four ACID properties mean in practice for an application that transfers money between accounts?
keyPoints: Atomicity: the debit and the credit both happen or neither does
Consistency: the constraints, such as foreign keys or a non-negative balance, hold before and after
Isolation: concurrent transfers do not see or disturb each other's unfinished work
Durability: a committed transfer survives a crash (the write-ahead log)

templates.question: Explain the isolation levels and the anomalies each one prevents. What does PostgreSQL use by default?
keyPoints: Anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads, lost updates and write skew
READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE prevent progressively more of them (PostgreSQL treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED)
PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED: each statement sees the data committed before it began
PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation: no phantoms, but write skew is possible
SERIALIZABLE detects conflicts and aborts a transaction, which the application must retry

templates.question: How does MVCC let readers and writers work at the same time in PostgreSQL, and what does VACUUM have to do with it?
keyPoints: An update writes a new version of the row instead of overwriting it
Each transaction sees a snapshot: the row versions committed before its snapshot was taken
Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers
Dead row versions pile up until VACUUM (autovacuum) reclaims them; it also prevents transaction-id wraparound
A long-running transaction keeps old versions alive and causes bloat

templates.question: Two requests read a product's stock of 10, each subtracts its quantity in Java and writes the result back. The final stock is wrong. How would you fix it?
keyPoints: A lost update: both read the same value and the second write overwrites the first
Update atomically in SQL: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - ? WHERE id = ? AND stock >= ?, and check the affected row count
Or lock the row first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
Or use optimistic locking with a version column and retry on conflict
SERIALIZABLE with retries also works

misconceptions: A SELECT always takes locks in PostgreSQL
A higher isolation level prevents deadlocks
Optimistic locking needs no handling in the application

templates.question: Compare optimistic and pessimistic locking. When would you choose each?
keyPoints: Pessimistic locking locks the row before changing it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), so others wait
It suits frequent conflicts and expensive retries, at the risk of waiting and deadlocks
Optimistic locking takes no lock and checks a version at update time (UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?)
A conflict makes the update fail, and the application must retry or report it
It suits rare conflicts and long user think times

templates.question: The logs show ERROR: deadlock detected for two transactions updating the same tables. How do you find the cause, and how do you prevent it?
keyPoints: Each transaction holds a lock the other one needs; PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one of them
The log entry names the statements and the locks involved
Prevent it by locking rows in a consistent order, for example by id
Keep transactions short, and retry the aborted transaction

templates.question: Several worker instances poll a jobs table for pending jobs, and sometimes two workers process the same job. How would you make picking up jobs safe with PostgreSQL?
keyPoints: Two workers read the same pending row before either marks it as taken
Claim jobs atomically inside a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n, then mark them running
SKIP LOCKED lets each worker take different rows without waiting
A single UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'PENDING' ... RETURNING also claims atomically
A lease or timeout returns the jobs of crashed workers

templates.question: What locks does an UPDATE take in PostgreSQL, and what happens to another transaction that updates the same row at the same time?
keyPoints: An UPDATE locks the rows it changes until its transaction ends
A second transaction updating the same row waits until the first commits or rolls back
Under READ COMMITTED it then re-checks the row and applies its update to the new version
Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE it fails with a serialization error instead
A plain SELECT takes no row locks
